thread.title: Apple Is Still Undervalued: Here's Why - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Investing City
title: Apple Is Still Undervalued: Here's Why - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Investment Thesis It’s baffling to think that a company as big, with such a cult following as Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) could see its stock nearly double in a year. If the market is truly efficient should a company be able to add nearly $450 billion of value in just 720 days? This article will argue that Apple’s stock, even though it has seen quite a rise, is still undervalued.
AAPL data by YCharts
The Rundown Nearly 2 million people have Apple in their portfolio on SeekingAlpha. It is the most followed stock. It has the biggest market cap of publicly traded companies and it will most likely be the first company to reach a $1 trillion market cap. Yet, it is still undervalued with all these eyes on it. Buffett can see it. He owns about 240 million shares. Here’s why it is still undervalued.
The Narrative Apple, until a few years ago, was reliant on iPhone sales. It was all about the iPhone. iPhone, iPhone, iPhone. Now it is all about the services segment. Rather than just focusing on phone sales, Apple has now built a sticky ecosystem of services, including the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, iCloud and AppleCare. But you know that don’t you? It is hard to write a story on Apple that everyone doesn’t already know. And most likely, this article won’t provide any details that absolutely blow you away. But maybe a slightly new perspective will do the trick.
By the Numbers The iPhone is still huge for Apple, don’t get me wrong. In just the first two quarters of the year, iPhone sales were just shy of $100 billion. That is surely nothing to sneeze at. The segment even saw 14% revenue growth thanks to a higher average selling price from upgrades to iPhone 8 and the iPhone X. But as stated, the real headline was the growth in services. This segment grew 31% year-over-year to $9.2 billion in the last reported quarter. Yes, that’s right, $9.2 billion in the quarter. To put that in perspective, Adobe (NASDAQ: ADBE ) did just $8 billion in sales…for the year. Apple’s services segment dwarfs that number.
Apple’s management has set a goal for $50 billion in services revenue by 2020. If we annualize that $9.2 billion, we get nearly $37 billion by the end of this year. So it would require almost 35% annual growth to reach $50 billion from there. Obviously this doesn’t take into account any sequential growth for the remainder of this year though. However, it’s a testament to just how big management thinks the services segment can grow.
To bring it back to Adobe, we’ll use it as a proxy to think about valuing Apple’s services because it also sells subscriptions and is a rather mature company. Apple doesn’t break out services margins so Adobe may be a reasonable substitute for margin profile. Plus, Adobe’s revenue is growing in the ballpark of 25%, which similar to Apple’s services. Adobe’s profit margin stands at a whopping 30%. So on $8 billion in revenue, it does about $2.4 billion in profit. Tack on a PE ratio of about 50 and you roughly get its market cap , which is $120 billion.
If we assume, $37 billion in revenue at the end of this year for services, using the same profit margins and valuation metric as Adobe, the value at the end of this year comes to $555 billion. What’s more is that the services are growing even faster than Adobe’s sales.
Calculations Ex. - $37 billion * 30% profit margins * 50 PE = $555 billion
Taking out Apple’s net cash position from its market cap , we get an enterprise value of $764 billion.
Ex. – $909 billion market cap - $145 billion in net cash = $764 billion enterprise value
So now we can do a little sum-of-the-parts analysis to figure out how much the market is valuing the rest of the business.
Ex. - $764 billion enterprise value - $555 billion services value = $209 billion left over value
Source: Apple Data Summary
Leftovers In the last four quarters, Apple has done $247 billion in revenue. If you subtract out the respective services sales, you get about $214 billion in sales. So the market is valuing Apple’s holy hardware at a whopping 1x sales. And it’s not like Apple doesn’t have any pricing power. The company is continually able to raise prices of new models and think of new ideas.
Moreover, in the last earnings call, Tim Cook stated, that
“We have the best pipeline of products and services we’ve ever had.”
Of course he’s going to say that but it still shows a sense of confidence in what they are doing from a new-product perspective.
To try and value the left-overs from an earnings angle, Apple has had a gross margin of around 38% for a while now. Presumably, the services segment ratchets that number up but considering it only accounts for 14% of revenue, probably not too much. So let’s say 35% gross margin. Clearly, Apple’s hardware has pricing power. Operating expenses have typically accounted for 12-14% of revenue, so we can estimate a 26% operating margin.
So on $214 billion in sales, a 26% operating margin, gives us almost $56 billion in EBIT. So that tells us that the market is valuing the hardware and other products segments at less than 4x EBIT. You read that right, 3.8 to be exact.
Source: Apple Consolidated Financials
For a company that just issued another $100 billion in buybacks, a world class brand, top notch management, and incredible employees, 4x EBIT on the holy iPhone, Mac, and iPad seems a little hard to believe. Granted, this scenario assumes that the services segment can continue its growth and a rich valuation but it seems decently conservative.
10x EBIT seems reasonable so that would fetch a value for the left-overs of $560 billion. Add that to $555 in services and we get $1.1 trillion in market cap, 22% upside for today’s prices. Not bad for a company that has all eyes on it.
To End Maybe you see Apple is a slightly different light, maybe not, but hopefully your perspective changed a little. I think Apple gets a bad rap because it is so big. It is hard to envision a $900 billion company doubling anytime soon, but look, it almost did just that in less than two years. As an investor, we don’t get any extra points for degrees of difficulty. And that’s precisely why Apple will continue to do well. It’s too easy, it’s overlooked because it’s so closely followed. Everyone thinks there is no advantage. But there just might be…
